prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

We consider statistical mechanics models of continuous height effective interfaces in the presence of a delta-pinning at height zero. There is a detailed mathematical understanding of the depinning transition in 2 dimensions without disorder. Then the variance of the interface height w.r.t. the Gibbs measure stays bounded uniformly in the volume for any positive pinning force and diverges like the logarithm of the pinning force when it tends to zero.   How does the presence of a quenched disorder term in the Hamiltonian modify this transition? We show that an arbitarily weak random field term is enough to beat an arbitrarily strong delta-pinning in 2 dimensions and will cause delocalization. The proof is based on a rigorous lower bound for the overlap between local magnetizations and random fields in finite volume. In 2 dimensions it implies growth faster than the volume which is a contradiction to localization. We also derive a simple complementary inequality which shows that in higher dimensions the fraction of pinned sites converges to one when the pinning force tends to infinity.

outputs.L1:
We consider statistical-mechanics models of continuous-height effective interfaces subject to delta-pinning at height zero. In two dimensions, the depinning transition in the absence of disorder is well understood mathematically: the variance of the interface height with respect to the Gibbs measure remains uniformly bounded in the volume for every positive pinning force and diverges logarithmically as the pinning force tends to zero.

How does the introduction of a quenched disorder term in the Hamiltonian modify this transition? We show that, in two dimensions, an arbitrarily weak random-field term is sufficient to overcome an arbitrarily strong delta-pinning force, thereby causing delocalization. The proof relies on a rigorous finite-volume lower bound for the overlap between local magnetizations and random fields. In two dimensions, this bound implies growth faster than the volume, contradicting localization. We also derive a simple complementary inequality showing that, in higher dimensions, the fraction of pinned sites converges to one as the pinning force tends to infinity.
outputs.L2:
We study statistical-mechanics models for effective interfaces with continuous heights subject to delta pinning at height zero. In two dimensions, the disorder-free depinning transition is mathematically well understood: for every strictly positive pinning strength, the height variance under the Gibbs measure remains uniformly bounded as the system volume increases, while it diverges logarithmically as the pinning strength approaches zero.

We ask how adding quenched disorder to the Hamiltonian changes this behavior. Our results show that, in two dimensions, even an arbitrarily weak random-field term can overcome delta pinning of any strength and delocalize the interface. The argument relies on a rigorous finite-volume lower bound for the overlap between the local magnetizations and the random fields. In two dimensions, this bound yields growth exceeding the volume, contradicting localization. We also establish a complementary elementary inequality showing that, in higher dimensions, the proportion of pinned sites approaches one as the pinning strength tends to infinity.
outputs.L3:
The study investigates continuous-height interface models subject to delta-pinning at height zero and quenched random fields. Delta-pinning energetically favors configurations in which the interface touches the zero-height plane, while the disorder introduces spatially varying local forces that compete with this tendency.

In two dimensions, the disorder-free model is localized by any positive pinning strength. Nevertheless, the localization becomes progressively weaker as the pinning force approaches zero: although the interface remains pinned for every positive value of the force, its height variance diverges logarithmically in the weak-pinning limit.

The situation changes fundamentally in the presence of quenched disorder. In two dimensions, even an arbitrarily weak random field is sufficient to overcome delta-pinning, regardless of how strong the pinning force is, and the interface delocalizes. The proof relies on a rigorous finite-volume lower bound for the overlap between local magnetizations and the random fields. This overlap grows with the system size in a way that is incompatible with localization, thereby establishing disorder-induced delocalization.

In higher dimensions, by contrast, sufficiently strong pinning dominates the competing effects: as the pinning force tends to infinity, the fraction of sites pinned at height zero converges to one. Thus, the results highlight a pronounced dimensional dependence in the competition between pinning, fluctuations, and quenched disorder.
outputs.L4:
Continuous-height interface models describe a fluctuating surface by assigning a real-valued height to each site of a lattice, with neighboring heights coupled through an elastic interaction. Delta-pinning introduces an energetic reward whenever the interface touches a preferred level, typically height zero. In the absence of disorder, sufficiently strong pinning can localize the interface near this level and produce a depinning transition as the pinning strength is varied. The study examines how this picture changes when the interface is also exposed to a quenched random field—that is, a spatially varying external field sampled once and then held fixed.

The analysis focuses on the relationship between the local magnetization, or disorder-dependent mean height, and the random field acting at each site. Rigorous overlap bounds show that, in two dimensions, the interface cannot remain strongly aligned with the pinning substrate in the presence of random-field fluctuations. Rare but unavoidable disorder fluctuations occur on all relevant length scales and overwhelm the energetic advantage supplied by the pinning potential. Consequently, every nonzero random-field strength destroys the localized phase: no matter how large the delta-pinning force is chosen, the interface ultimately delocalizes in the thermodynamic limit.

The behavior is fundamentally different in higher dimensions. There, sufficiently strong pinning can dominate the effects of quenched disorder. As the pinning force tends to infinity, the density of sites at the preferred height converges to one, meaning that almost the entire interface becomes pinned. Thus the results identify two dimensions as a critical setting in which arbitrarily weak random-field disorder eliminates localization, while higher-dimensional systems retain a strongly pinned regime. This establishes a sharp dimensional contrast in the competition among elasticity, substrate pinning, and quenched randomness.
outputs.L5:
“There,” said Gibbs, pointing toward the darkened house at the end of the street. “That’s where the signal came from.”

His team waited for instructions, but Gibbs was already moving. He crossed the road quietly, his eyes fixed on the broken upstairs window. The night was still—too still.

Then a light flickered behind the glass.

Gibbs stopped. “We’re not alone.”

A shadow passed across the window, and somewhere inside, a floorboard creaked. Gibbs reached for his weapon and nodded toward the door.

“Now,” he said.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write an abstract for a mathematical physics paper on continuous-height effective interface models with delta-pinning and quenched random fields, emphasizing delocalization in two dimensions and strong-pinning behavior in higher dimensions.
counterfactuals.output: We study continuous-height effective interface models with a convex gradient interaction, quenched random fields, and a delta-pinning potential favoring contact with a reference substrate. Our main results identify a sharp dimensional contrast in the competition between disorder and pinning. In two dimensions, quenched fluctuations prevent localization: for every finite pinning strength, the interface exhibits divergent height fluctuations and no positive mass is generated in the thermodynamic limit. The proof combines finite-volume free-energy estimates, disorder fluctuations, and multiscale control of pinned contacts. In dimensions \(d\ge 3\), by contrast, sufficiently strong delta-pinning dominates the random field. We establish localization around the substrate, a positive density of pinned sites, and exponential decay of correlations, uniformly in the volume and for a broad class of disorder distributions and uniformly convex interactions. These results clarify the lower-critical-dimensional role of \(d=2\) and provide a rigorous description of the strong-pinning phase in higher dimensions.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Summarize how quenched disorder modifies the depinning transition of a two-dimensional continuous interface with delta-pinning at zero, including the main proof idea and the higher-dimensional result.
counterfactuals.output:
For the homogeneous two-dimensional continuous interface with a hard wall and \(\delta\)-pinning at height \(0\), depinning is first order: at the critical pinning strength the contact fraction jumps from a positive value to zero.

Adding i.i.d. quenched randomness to the local pinning rewards rounds this transition. The quenched free energy is differentiable in the pinning parameter, so the contact density cannot jump at the quenched critical point. Thus disorder replaces phase coexistence/abrupt depinning by a continuous transition; it may also shift the critical point relative to the annealed or pure model.

The proof is an interface-specific version of the Aizenman–Wehr disorder-rounding argument. One assumes two phases with different contact densities coexist, then studies the free-energy change caused by resampling or perturbing the disorder in a large box. Coexistence would produce disorder-induced fluctuations of volume type, of order \(L^{d/2}\). Locality and comparison of boundary conditions bound the same free-energy difference by a surface term, of order \(L^{d-1}\). In \(d=2\) these scales are marginal, so a refined fluctuation/concentration argument yields the contradiction. Convexity of the free energy then converts the result into continuity of the contact density.

In dimensions \(d\ge 3\), the surface cost dominates the disorder fluctuations, so this rounding mechanism no longer applies. Indeed, for sufficiently weak disorder the first-order depinning transition survives: localized and delocalized phases coexist and the contact fraction retains a discontinuity.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate a research-paper abstract explaining why an arbitrarily weak random field can overcome arbitrarily strong delta-pinning in 2D, using a lower bound on the overlap between local magnetizations and random fields.
counterfactuals.output:
We study a two-dimensional lattice spin/interface model with a delta-pinning potential of arbitrary finite strength and an independent, centered random field of arbitrarily small amplitude. We prove that pinning cannot suppress the disorder-induced response in the thermodynamic limit. The key estimate is a quantitative lower bound on the disorder–magnetization overlap
\[
\mathbb E\!\left[\sum_{x\in\Lambda} h_x\,\langle m_x\rangle_h\right],
\]
where \(h_x\) is the local random field and \(\langle m_x\rangle_h\) is the corresponding quenched local magnetization. Convexity and multiscale fluctuation estimates show that, in two dimensions, favorable random-field fluctuations occur on every scale and yield a cumulative free-energy gain that eventually exceeds the finite energetic advantage produced by any fixed delta-pinning strength. Thus even when the disorder amplitude is arbitrarily small, sufficiently large scales contain regions in which the system profits from departing from the pinned state. This establishes a rigorous version of the marginal Imry–Ma mechanism: two-dimensional random-field fluctuations overwhelm arbitrarily strong but finite local pinning, precluding a uniformly pinned phase and forcing a nonvanishing disorder-aligned response.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Compare the localization behavior of delta-pinned effective interfaces with and without disorder in two dimensions, and briefly state what happens to the fraction of pinned sites under strong pinning in higher dimensions.
counterfactuals.output:
In two dimensions, a homogeneous (disorder-free) \(\delta\)-pinning potential localizes the interface for every positive pinning strength. With quenched disorder, weak pinning may no longer localize it; a genuine delocalized-to-localized transition occurs as the pinning strength is increased.

In higher dimensions, sufficiently strong pinning produces a positive macroscopic density of pinned sites, with the pinned fraction tending to \(1\) as the pinning strength becomes large.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Draft a concise technical overview of results for continuous-height Gibbs interfaces subject to delta-pinning and quenched disorder, mentioning variance behavior in the disorder-free case, disorder-induced delocalization in 2D, and the complementary inequality for higher dimensions.
counterfactuals.output:
For a continuous-height gradient Gibbs interface with \(\delta\)-pinning strength \(\varepsilon\), the disorder-free model is localized: the one-point variance remains bounded as the volume grows. In \(d=2\), this bound deteriorates only logarithmically as \(\varepsilon\downarrow0\), while in \(d\ge3\) it stays uniformly bounded, reflecting transience of the underlying walk.

Quenched disorder can destroy this localization in two dimensions. Under the usual nondegeneracy and moment assumptions on the disorder, the disorder-averaged quenched variance grows at least logarithmically with the linear size of the box; hence the pinned field is not tight and is delocalized.

In higher dimensions, the complementary comparison inequality bounds the quenched variance by the corresponding homogeneous—or effective massive Green-function—variance, up to constants determined by the disorder law and pinning parameters. Thus the two-dimensional divergence is critical, whereas for \(d\ge3\) the same estimates are compatible with bounded fluctuations and localization.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
